newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU plays dead at low-key grain export tender.
newsitem.headline: EU plays dead at low-key grain export tender.

text.p: The European Union all but slammed the door on grains exports on Thursday in a surprise move that owed as much to swirling currency movements as the fragile state of world prices, traders and officials said.
The EU's cereals committee in Brussels issued licences to export just 70,000 tonnes or so each of wheat and barley, with the maximum wheat export refund pegged at 14.50 Ecus per tonne.
"They've been a bit mean," one Swiss-based exporter said. "We'd expected them to give 16 Ecus to keep the (quantity exported) at around 230,000 tonnes."

With the dollar rising to its frothiest level since 1994, making European wheat more competitive, many traders expected the European Commission to be more generous with Ecu-denominated export subsidies to keep a bumper crop flowing at the ports.
But a growing surplus of southern hemisphere wheat and the sheer pace of the dollar's rally appeared to have made the EU's executive jumpy about joining in a market race, traders said.

An expanding U.S. economy has driven the dollar 6.4 percent up against the French franc, Europe's main grain currency, since the New Year, breaking through 5.50 francs for the first time since 1994. The gain since January 1996 is over 12 percent.
Meantime Australia's wheat crop, now being harvested, is set to reach a record of 23 million tonnes against normal output of 15-16 million tonnes, officials in Sydney said earlier.
At the same time the EU is trying to market its 1996 crop which also entered the record books despite drought in the central French grain belt last summer.
"The significant thing is that the trade is looking again at the situation and noticing there is plenty of wheat everywhere," one trade analyst said.
That lesson was underscored while the weekly EU export tender was happening on Thursday, with Tunisia buying 125,000 tonnes of wheat for about $158 with freight -- considered cheap.
The sale was done, probably at a loss, by long holders using it to liquidate positions cheaply, one European trader said.
Although the EU market is now felt to be somewhat short of export licences, few are expected to commit themselves to paying Commission prices for more than a month ahead, analysts said.
Thursday's EU wheat award was valued at $150-151 per tonne, fob France -- well above Tunisia's purchase in the $140s once freight is taken off.
Barley exports were also slow, forcing several traders to ponder whether the EU would miss out on recent large barley sales to Saudi Arabia.
Spain, with a large crop last year, is ready to load barley for the Gulf even without the special export terms it had hoped to get from the Commission this winter.

But although the highest subsidy bids of some 31 Ecus might have allowed that to happen, the Commission displayed a traditional reluctance to accept a wide gap between the lowest and highest subsidy bids, and put the cut-off below 28 Ecus.
Exporters are aware of this policy and occasionally send in low bids to encourage Brussels to cut off the refunds at a level lower than their rivals need to cover business, analysts said.
They said Canada and Australia looked increasingly likely to cover the bulk of the 1.2-million-tonne sale to Saudi Arabia.
